Q1089704.summary: Worked in relief rather than painted flat, this darkened and cracked icon shows the Virgin turned slightly toward the Christ Child, whom she holds on her left arm, her hand gesturing toward him. The Child, in red and blue garments, sits upright with a golden halo. Venerated as the Blachernitissa, a revered image linked with the great Marian shrine of Constantinople, it was brought from Mount Athos to Moscow in 1653, where Tsar Alexis received it in person.
facts: Tradition held that the icon was made of wax mixed with the ashes of martyrs.
Recent study has found close parallels with 13th-century relief icons and a newly discovered Greek inscription, so the 13th century is now regarded as its most likely date.
It was restored by Simon Ushakov and Nikita Pavlovets in 1674 and survived the Great Fire of Moscow in 1812.
Q1089704.notes: Wikidata and Commons give '7th century', but Wikipedia reports that scholarship now favours the 13th century; whether it is the icon once kept at Blachernae is disputed (that icon is thought to have been of the Orans type, while this one is a Hodegetria). This redating moves the work out of the 1st–7th-century batch. The phrasing 'survived the Great Fire' follows Wikipedia's statement that it was left in the Kremlin and put at risk in 1812.

cur:catacombs-stilicho-sarcophagus.summary: Beneath the Romanesque pulpit of Sant'Ambrogio, the sarcophagus shows Christ seated among his apostles before a city gate, with twelve sheep below, while other faces show Christ giving the law to Peter and the sacrifice of Isaac; the lid includes the Magi and an early Nativity. It is among the most refined sarcophagi of the Theodosian age.
facts: Wikipedia dates it to about 387–390, two decades before the general Stilicho's death, so it is unlikely to have been his.
It has served as the base of the pulpit of Sant'Ambrogio since before the 10th century.
Its carving has been estimated to have cost 50,000–100,000 Diocletianic denarii.

cur:objects-vam-hodegetria-statuette.summary: Carved fully in the round, the slender Mother of God stands holding the Christ Child on her left arm and gestures toward him with her right hand, showing him as the Way. The Child sits upright, holding a scroll and blessing. Almost unique as a freestanding Byzantine statuette, it preserves the form of the venerated Hodegetria icon in three dimensions.
facts: The V&A describes it as the sole surviving example of freestanding Byzantine ivory sculpture; it was probably placed in a small tabernacle so that it could be seen from all sides.

The head of the Christ Child is a 19th-century restoration, most probably made in the Castellani workshop in Rome; a lozenge pattern of dots on the Virgin's cloak suggests it was once painted and gilded.
It was bought from the collection of Alessandro Castellani in Rome in 1884.

Q5028815.summary: This rare free-standing cross from eastern Scotland is carved on every face. The face shown is usually interpreted as Christ flanked by angels at the head of the cross, above the four Evangelists on the shaft; on the badly weathered opposite face the antiquary Alexander Gordon recorded a Crucifixion in 1726. Its sculpture shows Irish influence and belongs to the last phase of Pictish carving.
facts: The Camus Cross and the Dupplin Cross are the only intact free-standing crosses of this period in eastern Scotland.
Local tradition held that it marked the grave of 'Camus', a Norse leader supposedly defeated by Malcolm II; the name more likely comes from the vanished village of Camuston.
Robert Maule, its earliest describer, read the main figure scene as Moses giving out the Law.
Q5028815.notes: The photograph appears to show the east face (Christ with angels and Evangelists); the Crucifixion face is largely weathered away.

walters:71.192.summary: This small ivory leaf, once one cover of a set of writing tablets, is carved in two registers beneath trefoil arches. Above, Christ kneels in prayer on the Mount of Olives while his disciples sleep, and beside it he is seized in the crowded scene of his arrest; below are the Annunciation and the Visitation. The back was hollowed to hold wax, so that a scene of Christ's agony accompanied everyday writing.
facts: The Walters notes a large hole drilled at the top for attaching the other cover and the tablets between, and a depression for wax on the back.

The museum relates its architecture of double trefoil arches to the so-called Atelier of the Boxes of the later 14th century, and its Annunciation and Visitation to a plaque in the Kofler Collection attributed to northern France or Flanders.
walters:71.192.notes: The worklist year (850) was wrong; the museum dates the tablet to the 4th quarter of the 14th century (Gothic).
